notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 39:23–43, drawn from the sources I was able to reach:

---

## Exodus 39:23–43 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 23 — The Reinforced Opening in the Robe

The robe of the ephod (the *me‘îl*) was woven all of blue and made in one piece. It had an opening at the top centre for the head, described as being “like the opening of a coat of mail” (KJV: “habergeon”). This comparison suggests a reinforced neck-hole bound with a woven collar or hem so that the fabric would not tear when the priest put it on or took it off.

- **Adam Clarke** (Methodist) explains that a “habergeon” or hauberk was a small coat of mail made of interlocking iron rings covering the neck and breast, borrowed by Norman crusaders from the ancient Persians. The opening in the priestly robe was similarly reinforced.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/39-23.html

- **Matthew Henry** (Puritan/evangelical) draws a Christological lesson: the robe—like all the priestly garments—was a shadow of Christ, our great High Priest, who “put on the clothes of service” and arrayed Himself with the gifts of the Spirit.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

- **Keil & Delitzsch** (Lutheran) note that the robe (*me‘îl*) was an upper garment, closely fitting, reaching to the knees, made of one piece. The binding around the opening prevented tearing, and the robe was not a covering for the ephod but worn under it.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

---

### v. 24 — Pomegranates on the Hem

On the lower hem of the robe, the craftsmen made artificial pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn twisted together with fine linen.

- **Ellicott** says the pomegranates were of blue, purple, and scarlet “twisted together” (not separate colours side by side but combined).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/39.htm

- **The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary** links the pomegranate fringe to Numbers 15:38–39, where every Israelite was commanded to wear a blue fringe to remember the commandments. The pomegranates on Aaron’s robe signified that his high-priestly service was not to follow his own course but to conform exactly to God’s regulations. Some also suggested the pomegranates symbolised fragrance and fruitfulness of priestly service done according to God’s will.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/39-24.html

- **Jonathan Edwards**, quoted in the *Expositor’s Dictionary of Texts*, sees the pomegranates as representing the fruit that saints bring forth, and the bells as their good profession: “The fruit they bring forth in life evermore answers the pleasant sound of their profession.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/edt/exodus/39.htm

---

### v. 25 — Bells of Pure Gold

The workers made bells of pure gold and placed them on the hem of the robe between the pomegranates.

- **Ellicott** defers the meaning of the bells to the note on Exodus 28:35 (not fetched, but the traditional reading is clear from other sources).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-25.htm

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** states the bells were designed to let the people outside know that the high priest was still alive as he ministered inside the tabernacle. There were no windows; the sound of bells was the only reassurance.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/ghb/exodus-39.html

---

### v. 26 — Alternating Bells and Pomegranates

A bell and a pomegranate alternated all around the hem. The phrase “to minister in” (or “for the service”) indicates this was the garment worn when the high priest performed his duties.

- **The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary** surveys several traditional interpretations of the bells’ meaning and finds most “fanciful.” It settles on the view tied to Hebrews 7:25: the tinkling bells proclaimed that the high priest was still alive inside the veil, interceding — and thus they are a type of Christ’s ongoing intercession. If the bells stopped, it meant the priest was dead (cf. Exodus 28:35: “that he die not”).  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/39-26.html

- **Keil** (as reported by the Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary) saw the bells as symbolising the sounding forth of the Word of God. **Lange** saw the alternation as signifying the connection of nature and grace. But the dominant evangelical reading ties them to the assurance of the living intercessor.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/39-26.html

- **Dr. Constable** (Dispensational) simply notes the repetition of the refrain “as the LORD had commanded Moses” — the seventh such occurrence in the chapter, emphasising precise obedience.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/dcc/exodus-39.html

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)** takes the Pentecostal/charismatic line: the bells served a functional purpose during worship, announcing the priest’s movement in the holy place. No additional symbolic overlay is stressed.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-39/

---

### v. 27 — Tunics of Fine Linen

Tunics for Aaron and his sons were made of fine linen, the work of a weaver. These were the long undercoat worn by all priests.

- **Keil & Delitzsch** note these were “body-coats” worn by both Aaron and the ordinary priests. The linen signified purity and holiness.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

- **Matthew Henry** observes that the clean linen with which the priests’ clothes of service were made represents “the righteousness of saints” (Revelation 19:8).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

- **Gill** (Baptist) notes that the linen material for the ordinary priests’ coats is specified here, whereas it was not in the earlier instructions — expressive of their purity before God and man. He adds that even heathen priests (e.g., Egyptian priests of Isis) wore only linen, a practice possibly imitated from this.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

---

### v. 28 — Turban, Ornate Headbands, Undergarments

These items were all of fine linen. The high priest’s turban (*miṣnepheṯ*) and the ordinary priests’ “goodly bonnets” or “ornamental caps” (*migbā‘ōṯ pĕ’ērî*) are distinguished. The undergarments (linen breeches) were for modesty.

- **Keil & Delitzsch** point out that the ordinary priests’ head-dresses in Exodus 28:40 are called simply “bonnets,” but here they are “goodly bonnets” (ornamental caps), the Hebrew *pĕ’ēr* meaning “ornament.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

- **The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary** notes the breeches, bonnets, and linen coats were articles Aaron wore in common with the entire priestly order and call for no special symbolic note beyond general purity.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/39-30.html

---

### v. 29 — The Embroidered Sash

The sash was of finely spun linen, embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn.

- **Keil & Delitzsch** discuss a textual subtlety: the singular “girdle” with the definite article in Hebrew might seem to refer only to Aaron’s sash, but since no separate description exists for the ordinary priests’ sashes, the singular is probably a collective or generic noun — the sashes were all of the same materials and make.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

- This is the sixth occurrence of “as the LORD had commanded Moses” in the chapter, again underscoring exact obedience.

---

### v. 30 — The Plate of the Holy Crown

A plate of pure gold was fashioned and engraved like a signet seal with the words: “HOLY TO THE LORD” (or “HOLINESS TO THE LORD”). This was the “holy crown” (*nēzer haqqōdeš*), the frontlet worn on Aaron’s turban.

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown** note that the seal-ring worn by ancient Egyptians on the little finger often bore a religious sentiment or sacred symbol. The inscription on the high priest’s plate alludes to this practice.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-30.htm

- **Precept Austin** cites Currid: this plate is “a fitting finale to the construction of the items for the tabernacle, for the plate has on it an inscription that says, ‘Holy to Yahweh’ — and that is one of the most important points about the entire tabernacle construction. It is set apart to Yahweh, for his worship and his service.”  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-39-commentary

- **The Hebrew term *nēzer*** (from *nāzar*, to dedicate/consecrate) speaks of separation or dedication. Precept Austin notes it is used both for the priest’s golden plate and for the Nazirite’s hair — both signs of consecration.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-29-commentary

- **The Preacher’s Homiletical Commentary** draws out three symbolic ideas: (1) *Personal consecration* — Aaron was crowned as the sanctified of the Lord. (2) *Representative propitiation* — wearing the crown, Aaron bore the iniquity of the people’s holy offerings. (3) *Congregational acceptance* — when Aaron appeared before God with the holy crown, the people were accepted. All three point to Christ, who is personally holy, makes expiation, and secures acceptance for His people.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/39-30.html

---

### v. 31 — The Blue Cord to Mount the Plate

A blue cord fastened the gold plate to the front of the turban, just as the LORD had commanded.

- **Ellicott** notes that the instruction to fasten it “on high” (i.e., on the front of the turban) was not explicit in the original command in Exodus 28:37, which only ordered that it be placed “in front.” The execution account adds this detail.  
  https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-30.htm

- **Matthew Henry** sees Christ in this: “He crowned himself with holiness to the Lord, consecrating his whole undertaking to the honour of his Father’s holiness.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-23.htm

---

### v. 32 — All the Work Completed

With this verse the narrative shifts from the garments to the entire tabernacle project. “So all the work for the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, was completed.” This echoes the language of Genesis 2:1–2 (creation completed).

- **Dr. Constable** notes that the statement “they did their work just as God had commanded Moses” brackets the section (v. 32 and v. 42), forming an inclusio. The completion language deliberately parallels the Creation narrative.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/dcc/exodus-39.html

- **Keil & Delitzsch** estimate the whole work was accomplished “in rather less than half a year” (see Exodus 40:17, where the tabernacle was erected on the first day of the first month of the second year), which they take as a most cheering sign of Israel’s willingness to serve the Lord.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-43.htm

---

### vv. 33–41 — The Inventory Brought to Moses

These verses list everything brought to Moses for inspection. The list is comprehensive and follows closely the order of the earlier instructions.

- **The Pulpit Commentary** says each item was brought “as it was finished” and judged by Moses “according to the pattern which he had seen upon the mount” (Exodus 25:40). If anything was disapproved, it would have been rejected — but no disapproval is recorded.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/tpc/exodus-39.html

- **Matthew Henry** sees the inventory as proof that they “had made all, omitting nothing,” and that Moses’ inspection verified every detail against the divine pattern.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/39-32.html

- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary** notes that the tabernacle parts were completed but *not yet assembled*. Moses would supervise the erection in chapter 40.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/bbc/exodus-39.html

---

### v. 42 — Done Just as the LORD Commanded

This verse repeats the key refrain: “The Israelites had done all the work just as the LORD had commanded Moses.”

- **Gill** emphasises that the obedience was complete “both as to matter and manner in every point,” made possible because the workers were “filled by the Spirit of God with wisdom and understanding.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-43.htm

- **Constable** notes this forms the closing bracket of the inclusio begun in v. 32.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/dcc/exodus-39.html

---

### v. 43 — Moses Inspects and Blesses

Moses examined all the work, found it exactly conforming to God’s command, and blessed the people.

- **Ellicott**: Moses inspected “to see if it was ‘according to the pattern’ shown him. Being satisfied, he expressed his own and God’s approval by blessing those who had worked so faithfully.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-43.htm

- **Benson** (Methodist): “For the same that showed him the pattern, guided their hand in the work.” Moses blessed them “not only praised them, but prayed for them: he blessed them as one having authority.” He adds that no wages were paid — the honour of God’s tabernacle among them and the blessing itself were recompense enough.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-43.htm

- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: This was a formal inspection conducted “not only with a view to have the work transferred from the charge of the workmen, but to ascertain whether it corresponded with ‘the pattern.’” Every item proved accurate, and Moses “thanked God for them, and begged Him to bless them.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-43.htm

- **Gill**: Moses “commended them for what they had done, and implored the divine blessing upon them.” He cites the Targum of Jonathan, which gives the form of the blessing: “May the Shechinah of the Lord dwell in the works of your hands,” and notes Jarchi’s version adds words from Psalm 90:17: “and the beauty of the Lord our God may be upon us.”  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-43.htm

- **Clarke** (Methodist): Moses acted as “the general superintendent of the whole, under whom Bezaleel and Aholiab were employed.”  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/acc/exodus-39.html

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)**: “Moses was the leader with the command from God and with the best knowledge of the pattern God wanted the tabernacle built according to … This was wonderful obedience. No wonder Moses blessed them.”  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-39/

- **Matthew Henry** adds a typological flourish: the tabernacle was a type of Jesus Christ (Colossians 2:9), of every believer in whom the Father dwells, of the church, and of the heavenly temple (Revelation 21:3).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/39-43.htm

- **Constable** notes the deliberate echo of the creation narrative: just as God blessed after creation (Genesis 1:28), Moses blesses after the completion of the tabernacle.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/eng/dcc/exodus-39.html

---

## Traditions Compared

**The main interpretive divide** in these verses is not between Protestant denominational traditions — all essentially agree on the historic-grammatical meaning — but in how much typological weight is placed on the details:

| Tradition | Emphasis |
|-----------|----------|
| **Reformed / Puritan** (Matthew Henry, Gill, JFB) | Heavy Christological typology: every garment detail points to Christ as High Priest; the linen is the righteousness of saints; the crown-plate is Christ’s holiness |
| **Lutheran** (Keil & Delitzsch) | Careful philological and historical detail; the blue robe indicates “the heavenly origin and character of the office”; the seamless robe sets forth “spiritual wholeness or integrity” |
| **Methodist / Wesleyan** (Clarke, Benson) | Historical background (e.g., habergeon as Persian armour) combined with practical application; stress on Moses’ blessing as “wages enough” |
| **Baptist** (Gill, Garner-Howes) | Gill focuses on rabbinic sources and historical parallels; Garner-Howes makes a direct Christological link from the bells to “the witness of His Spirit that Christ is still alive as our High Priest” |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik) | Generally stays close to the plain sense; emphasises obedience and the Spirit’s empowerment of the craftsmen; less elaborate typology |
| **Dispensational** (Constable) | Notes structural features (the inclusio, the Creation parallel, the sevenfold “as the LORD commanded”); sees the tabernacle as a type of Christ in a dispensational framework |

No distinctively **Catholic**, **Orthodox**, or **modern critical** sources were retrieved within the search limits. The **NET Bible** notes and **Bible Odyssey** could not be reached. No prosperity-gospel or hyper-grace readings appeared in any of the pages searched — these traditions typically do not produce detailed commentaries on Exodus 39.

---

## Summary

The great unifying theme across all traditions for Exodus 39:23–43 is **exact obedience to the divine pattern**. The craftsmen made everything — robe with bells and pomegranates, tunics, turban, sash, holy crown — precisely as the LORD had commanded. Moses inspected every piece and found it faithful. His blessing on the people is the climax of the whole construction narrative, deliberately echoing God’s blessing at creation. Across traditions, the typological arrow points to Christ: our living High Priest whose ongoing intercession is signalled by the bells, whose perfect holiness is inscribed on His brow, and whose finished work secures the blessing of God for His people.
